title: The One I Refuse to Pity
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 25 of 40
content:
The Daily Prophet printed a photograph of Snape under the headline MONSTER, MARTYR, OR BOTH?

He threw the paper into the fire.

I rescued it.

“Why?” he demanded.

“Evidence of bad punctuation.”

“There is no punctuation in the headline.”

“Exactly.”

He stared.

I folded the paper and put it in my case.

The article was worse than the headline.

It described Snape as a tragic figure, a secret hero, a cruel teacher, a love-struck recluse, a former terrorist, a tortured genius, and—most offensively to him—“the broken man who never recovered from losing his childhood sweetheart.”

Snape read that line twice.

Then he laughed so coldly I felt sorry for the journalist.

“Broken,” he said.

“Journalists like simple nouns.”

“And childhood sweetheart.”

“That is inaccurate?”

“It is idiotic.”

“Fair.”

He stalked across the laboratory.

I waited for the anger to spend itself.

It did not.

“They know nothing,” he said.

“No.”

“They take one memory and build a religion from it.”

“Yes.”

“They speak of grief as though it were romantic constancy instead of—”

He stopped.

“Instead of what?”

His face tightened.

“Complicated.”

“That word again.”

“You overuse it.”

“You embody it.”

His lip curled.

I took the paper back out.

“Do you want to respond?”

“No.”

“Do you want me to burn it now?”

“Yes.”

I held it over the fire.

Then paused.

“What?” he snapped.

“I want to ask something first.”

“Of course you do.”

“Do you think loving Lily ruined your life?”

The anger vanished.

Snape stared at me.

“That is not what the article says.”

“I know.”

“You are extrapolating.”

“Yes.”

His face closed.

I nearly let it go.

Then he said, “No.”

I waited.

“Losing her did not ruin my life,” he said. “My choices did considerable work before that.”

There was the familiar cruelty toward himself, but also something more balanced beneath it.

“And loving her?”

His gaze moved toward the window.

“Loving her saved parts of it.”

The answer was beautiful because it was not clean.

I burned the newspaper.

The flames took monster first, then martyr.

Snape watched.

“I refuse to pity you,” I said.

His eyebrow lifted.

“What an extraordinary gift.”

“I mean it.”

“I know. That is what makes it extraordinary.”

I stepped closer.

“I feel compassion for you sometimes.”

“How unfortunate.”

“I feel angry on your behalf sometimes.”

“Worse.”

“I think some things that happened to you were terrible.”

“You are approaching sentimentality.”

“And I still refuse to pity you.”

His expression sharpened.

“Why?”

“Because pity puts you below me.”

That stopped him.

“I don't want you below me,” I continued. “I want you beside me.”

Silence.

The words came out more intimate than I expected.

Snape's eyes locked on mine.

I could hear the fire behind us.

I could hear my own pulse.

Beside me.

Not save you.

Not fix you.

Not forgive you for things that were not mine to forgive.

Beside me.

Snape took one step forward.

Now we were too close for pretense.

“Do you?” he asked.

His voice was barely above a whisper.

“Yes.”

“You have poor judgment.”

“Established.”

“You have seen enough to know that.”

“Yes.”

“You are still here.”

“Yes.”

His hand lifted.

Stopped beside my face.

“May I?”

Every thought in my head disappeared.

I nodded.

“Say it.”

The demand was soft.

Consent mattered to him in language.

Maybe because so much of his life had been built around coercion, orders, secrets, things no one could safely refuse.

“Yes.”

His fingers touched my cheek.

Nothing more.

No kiss.

Just the back of his knuckles against my skin, careful enough to break me open.

I leaned into the touch.

Snape inhaled sharply.

His thumb moved once below my cheekbone.

“You are real,” he said.

I blinked.

“So are you.”

His mouth twisted.

“Debatable.”

I laughed softly.

The tension eased without disappearing.

His hand stayed.

“I thought,” he said, “that once you saw enough, this would correct itself.”

“This?”

“Your attraction.”

I smiled.

“That is incredibly insulting.”

“It was intended as self-criticism.”

“You're bad at keeping those separate.”

“I am learning.”

The honesty of it made my chest ache.

I raised my own hand, giving him enough time to refuse.

He did not.

I touched the side of his face.

His eyes closed.

That nearly undid me.

Snape, who watched everything.

Snape, who slept with a wand close enough to wake armed.

Snape closed his eyes under my hand.

Trust could be very quiet.

I stroked my thumb once along his cheek.

His skin was cool. A little rough. Human.

When he opened his eyes again, there was desire in them.

No mistaking it.

My breath caught.

His gaze dropped to my mouth.

Then returned to my eyes.

He stepped back.

I let him.

The absence of contact hurt immediately.

“Not yet,” he said.

I nodded.

“Okay.”

Surprise crossed his face.

“What?”

“You agree rather readily.”

“You said not yet, not convince me.”

His expression softened.

“Yes.”

I turned toward the worktable, giving both of us something else to look at.

“Also, the aconite needs sorting.”

Snape made a sound of disbelief.

“You are changing the subject to aconite.”

“You started this relationship with bitterroot.”

“We do not have a relationship.”

I looked over my shoulder.

His face changed.

I smiled.

“No?”

Snape stared at me.

Then, very slowly, his mouth curved.

“Sort the aconite.”

“Coward.”

“Consultant.”

“Prince.”

His eyes warmed.

We sorted aconite.

The newspaper turned to ash behind us.

Monster and martyr disappeared together.

The almost-kiss followed me for the rest of the afternoon.

It lived in absurd places: between ingredient counts, in the pause before a cabinet opened, in the half second when Severus passed behind my chair and his sleeve brushed my shoulder.

Neither of us mentioned it.

Eventually I put down my quill.

“This is ridiculous.”

“What is?”

“You know.”

“I am not responsible for every undefined discomfort you experience.”

“You touched my face.”

His quill stopped.

“Ah,” he said.

“Ah?”

“A highly technical response.”

I stared at him until he sighed.

“I did not stop because I did not want to kiss you.”

My pulse jumped.

“Then why?”

“Because I wanted to be certain the moment was not powered by pity, crisis, gratitude, or your appalling desire to rehabilitate difficult men.”

“I do not have an appalling desire to rehabilitate difficult men.”

His eyebrow rose.

“Fine. One difficult man.”

“That is not reassuring.”

I smiled despite the heat in my face.

“For the record,” I said, “I wanted to kiss you because you're infuriating.”

“Excellent. Romance restored to its proper foundation.”

The tension broke just enough for us to breathe.

Not yet, I understood, was not the same as no.

The man remained.
